blocks.text: Cirrhosis is **diffuse fibrosis of the whole liver with regenerative nodules**. It is a **histological** diagnosis, and it is the **commonest cause of portal hypertension**. Clinically, hepatocyte loss followed by scarring and nodules wrecks the normal architecture, so liver cell function fails and portal pressure rises.

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.title: How fibrosis develops
items: Liver injury → Kupffer cells and hepatocytes release cytokines
These activate **stellate cells in the space of Disse**, which turn into myofibroblast-like cells and lay down collagen
Removing the cause early (e.g. curing viral hepatitis) can clear fibrosis completely; established cirrhosis can only **regress**, not fully reverse

blocks.title: Histological patterns
rows: Small and uniform, about 1 mm across (Davidson)
Larger, of varying size, with broad scars where the architecture collapsed
Seen occasionally; no single typical cause

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.text: **Compensated vs decompensated.** Davidson uses "decompensated" (chronic liver failure) when the liver's metabolic reserve is exhausted, shown by **encephalopathy and/or ascites**. Quick-reference texts also count **variceal bleeding** as decompensation.

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.title: Causes of cirrhosis
rows: Chronic hepatitis B or C, prolonged heavy alcohol use, NAFLD
Autoimmune hepatitis, primary biliary cholangitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, secondary biliary cirrhosis
Haemochromatosis, Wilson's disease, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, cystic fibrosis
Budd–Chiari, right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome
About 15%; much of this is now thought to be burnt-out NAFLD

blocks.text: **Viral hepatitis is the leading cause worldwide**; in the West alcohol currently leads but NAFLD is expected to overtake it. Every patient with cirrhosis needs a search for a **treatable** cause.

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.text: In a **young** patient with cirrhosis always check **copper/caeruloplasmin and α1-antitrypsin**, plus iron studies for haemochromatosis.
Nodule size cut-off differs: **Davidson says micronodules are about 1 mm**, whereas Kumar & Clark use **< 3 mm**. Quote Davidson in the exam and recognise the other figure.

blocks.note: Compare: normal lobule → bridging fibrosis joining portal tracts and hepatic veins → cirrhosis with regenerative nodules ringed by fibrous bands.
Cirrhosis histology with nodules surrounded by fibrosis (collagen stain), and CT showing an irregular liver outline, varices and ascites.

blocks.text: Presentation ranges from an **incidental finding** in a well patient to vague symptoms: fatigue, weakness, muscle cramps, weight loss, anorexia, nausea and upper abdominal discomfort. The liver is **enlarged early** (especially alcohol and haemochromatosis) and **shrinks** as disease advances (especially viral and autoimmune); it feels **hard, irregular and non-tender**.

blocks.title: Signs of chronic liver disease
rows: Palmar erythema, clubbing, leuconychia, asterixis (flap), Dupuytren's contracture
Jaundice, spider telangiectasia, bruising/purpura, pigmentation, scratch marks
Gynaecomastia, testicular atrophy, impotence, loss of male hair pattern
Breast atrophy, irregular menses or amenorrhoea
Large or small liver, splenomegaly, ascites, dilated abdominal veins / caput medusae

blocks.text: **Spider telangiectasia**: a central arteriole with radiating vessels, 1–2 mm across, usually above the nipples. One or two are seen in about **2% of healthy people** and in pregnancy; otherwise they point strongly to liver disease.

Florid spiders, gynaecomastia and parotid enlargement suggest **alcohol** as the cause. Gynaecomastia may simply be due to **spironolactone**. The link with Dupuytren's contracture rests on weak evidence. Many cirrhotic patients have **few signs**.

blocks.title: Blood tests
items: **Albumin and prothrombin time** are the best guides to synthetic function; aminotransferases may be normal in compensated cirrhosis
Low sodium marks severe disease (fluid retention)
**Thrombocytopenia** from hypersplenism is common, usually around 100 × 10⁹/L
AST tends to exceed ALT in late disease
INR correlates poorly with actual bleeding risk

blocks.text: A prolonged PT caused by **liver damage is not corrected by vitamin K**. Vitamin K does correct it when the cause is malabsorption of the vitamin, e.g. biliary obstruction.

blocks.title: Imaging, fibrosis tests & biopsy
items: Ultrasound: nodular surface, splenomegaly, ascites, wide portal vein with sluggish flow
Non-invasive fibrosis tests (ELF, Fibrotest, FIB-4, Fibroscan elastography) have a **high negative but low positive predictive value**; Fibroscan is less reliable in obesity
ELF score: < 7.7 none–mild fibrosis; ≥ 9.8 severe fibrosis
Liver biopsy remains the gold standard, though samples may fragment in macronodular cirrhosis
Percutaneous biopsy needs **PT < 4 s prolonged and platelets > 80 × 10⁹/L**; otherwise use the **transjugular** route

blocks.title: Grading and prognosis
items: Child–Pugh total: **< 7 = A, 7–9 = B, > 9 = C**; 1-year survival roughly 100%, 80% and 45%
**MELD** adds **renal function (creatinine)**, which Child–Pugh lacks; it also uses bilirubin, INR and sodium
Bad signs: rising bilirubin, albumin < 30 g/L, sodium < 120 mmol/L (not diuretic-related), prolonged PT
Overall only **25% survive 5 years** from diagnosis (50% if liver function is good)

blocks.text: Quoted 5-year survival differs: Davidson gives **25% overall** (50% with good function); some quick sources say about 50%. Use Davidson's figure.

blocks.note: CT of cirrhosis: small irregular liver, splenomegaly, ascites around the liver and collateral vessels near the upper stomach.

cite.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.note: Body diagram of chronic liver disease signs, split into compensated and decompensated features.

blocks.text: Portal pressure is estimated by the **hepatic venous pressure gradient** (wedged minus free hepatic venous pressure). Normal is **5–6 mmHg**; portal hypertension is clinically significant **above 10 mmHg**, and variceal bleeding becomes likely **above 12 mmHg**.

blocks.title: Causes by site of obstruction
rows: ≥ 90% of adult cases in developed countries

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.title: Clinical features
items: **Splenomegaly** is the cardinal sign; portal hypertension is unlikely without it
Collaterals form at portosystemic junctions: lower oesophagus/gastric fundus, rectum, and around the umbilicus (**caput medusae**)
A venous hum over the umbilical collaterals = Cruveilhier–Baumgarten syndrome
Rectal varices are easily mistaken for haemorrhoids
Hypersplenism: platelets usually about 100 × 10⁹/L; < 50 is unusual. Anaemia should prompt a search for bleeding

blocks.title: Natural history and screening
items: About 90% of cirrhotic patients develop varices within 10 years, but only a third bleed
2-year bleeding risk: **7% for small, up to 30% for large varices**
Mortality after a bleed is about **15% overall but about 45% in Child–Pugh C**
Screening **endoscopy at diagnosis of cirrhosis, repeated every 2 years**

blocks.title: Primary prevention (varices that have never bled)
items: **Propranolol 80–160 mg/day** or nadolol, aiming to cut the resting heart rate by **25%**
Carvedilol 6.25–12.5 mg/day is an alternative and may be better tolerated
Propranolol reduces variceal bleeding by about 47%
**Band ligation** if β-blockers are not tolerated

blocks.title: Acute variceal bleed (Davidson Box 22.32)
rows: IV fluids / blood (target Hb about 80 g/L, avoid over-transfusion)
Restore circulation without raising portal pressure
Lowers portal pressure, controls bleeding, reduces mortality
Sepsis and SBP are common; antibiotics improve survival
About 20% are bleeding from a non-variceal lesion

blocks.title: Drug doses and rescue options
items: Terlipressin **2 mg IV four times daily** until bleeding stops, then 1 mg four times daily for up to 72 h; use with caution in severe ischaemic heart or peripheral vascular disease. Where terlipressin is not available, octreotide is the usual alternative
**Gastric fundal varices**: cyanoacrylate glue or thrombin injection (risk of glue embolism to the lungs)
**Sengstaken–Blakemore tube**: secure the airway first; gastric balloon 200–250 mL air; oesophageal balloon ≤ 40 mmHg, deflated for 10 min every 3 h; only a bridge
**TIPSS**: a stent between portal and hepatic veins placed via the jugular vein; less rebleeding than endoscopy but **no survival gain** and may cause encephalopathy
Pre-emptive TIPSS within 72 h benefits high-risk patients, mainly Child–Pugh C

blocks.title: Secondary prevention
items: Without it, **60–80% rebleed within 2 years**
Combine a non-selective β-blocker with **repeated banding every 2–4 weeks** until the varices are obliterated

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.text: **Portal hypertensive ("snakeskin") gastropathy**: multiple areas of punctate erythema in a congested stomach that causes chronic iron-deficiency anaemia. First-line treatment is propranolol; TIPSS if that fails.
Always endoscope a cirrhotic who bleeds: about **1 in 5 is bleeding from something other than varices**, such as a peptic ulcer.
First-line vasoactive drug differs between texts: UK sources (Davidson) use **terlipressin**, whereas US texts favour **octreotide**. Davidson keeps octreotide as the alternative.

blocks.note: Diagram of portal hypertension by site: pre-hepatic, pre-sinusoidal, sinusoidal and post-hepatic.
Endoscopy: oesophageal varices, gastric varices, and oesophageal varices after banding.
Algorithm for acute variceal bleeding: drugs and antibiotics → endoscopy and banding → balloon tamponade or TIPSS if haemostasis fails.
Sengstaken–Blakemore tube: identify the gastric and oesophageal balloons and the aspiration ports.
Radiograph of a TIPSS stent running from the portal vein to the hepatic vein.

blocks.text: **Why cirrhotics get ascites:** splanchnic vasodilatation (mainly nitric oxide) leaves the arterial circulation underfilled → **renin–angiotensin–aldosterone, sympathetic and ADH activation** → renal salt and water retention. Portal hypertension and low albumin then push the fluid into the peritoneum.

blocks.title: Detecting ascites
items: Clinically detectable from about **1 L**: flank fullness and **shifting dullness**; a fluid thrill when it is marked
Also: everted umbilicus, herniae, scrotal oedema, dilated abdominal veins (if portal hypertension)
**Ultrasound** is the best way to detect it and picks up very small volumes

blocks.title: Diagnostic tap – what each test tells you
items: **SAAG** (serum albumin − ascitic albumin) **> 11 g/L** → portal hypertension (about 96% accurate)
Total protein < 25 g/L in cirrhosis; > 25 g/L with a high SAAG suggests cardiac failure or hepatic outflow block
Neutrophils > 250 × 10⁶/L → infection (SBP); send culture in blood-culture bottles
Amylase > 1000 U/L → pancreatic ascites; triglyceride > 1.1 g/L → chylous ascites
Low glucose → malignancy or TB; cytology for malignant cells
A **bloody tap** in a cirrhotic signals **HCC** in about a third

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.title: Causes of ascites by SAAG
rows: High SAAG, protein usually > 25 g/L (venous outflow block)
Cardiac failure, constrictive pericarditis, Budd–Chiari syndrome, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome
Peritoneal or hepatic malignancy, tuberculous peritonitis, pancreatitis, lymphatic obstruction (chylous ascites); rarely hypothyroidism
Nephrotic syndrome, protein-losing enteropathy, malnutrition – placed differently by different books (see pitfall below)
Meigs' syndrome: benign ovarian tumour with a right pleural effusion, with or without ascites; resolves when the tumour is removed

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.text: Where **nephrotic syndrome** and other low-albumin states sit differs: Kumar & Clark, K&C Essentials and Pocket Medicine put them in the **low-SAAG** group, whereas Davidson's Box 22.21 puts hypoproteinaemia with the transudative (**high-SAAG**) causes. Do not use them as a deciding clue.

blocks.title: Stepwise treatment of cirrhotic ascites
rows: About 100 mmol/day (no added salt); avoid NSAIDs and sodium-rich drugs (effervescent tablets, antacids)
100–400 mg/day, first-line; switch to **amiloride 5–10 mg/day** for painful gynaecomastia or hyperkalaemia
If response is poor; watch electrolytes and renal function
Weight should fall by **no more than 1 kg/day**
No response to spironolactone 400 mg + furosemide 160 mg, or cannot tolerate them
First-line for refractory ascites, with **albumin 6–8 g per litre removed** (about 100 mL of 20–25% HAS per 1.5–2 L)
Alternative to repeated taps; does not prolong life and may worsen encephalopathy

blocks.title: When to stop diuretics (Kumar)
items: Rising creatinine, hyperkalaemia, worsening encephalopathy, or sodium < 128 mmol/L
Circulatory dysfunction after paracentesis is likelier when > 5 L is removed

blocks.text: Once cirrhotic ascites appears, only **10–20% survive 5 years**.
Thresholds differ: Davidson restricts water below **125 mmol/L** and gives **6–8 g albumin per litre**; Kumar uses **128 mmol/L** and **8 g/L**. Quote Davidson.
About 10% have a **right-sided pleural effusion** (hepatic hydrothorax). Do not blame a **left-sided** effusion on the ascites – investigate it.

blocks.note: Flow chart: splanchnic vasodilatation → underfilling → RAAS activation → salt and water retention, with portal hypertension and hypoalbuminaemia adding to it.

blocks.text: **SBP** is infection of ascites with no obvious intra-abdominal source. It affects up to 18% of decompensated patients with ascites. Organisms are enteric and reach the fluid via the blood – **E. coli** most often, also Klebsiella and enterococci. Classic features are pain, rebound, absent bowel sounds and fever, but in about **one-third abdominal signs are mild or absent** and the picture is **encephalopathy plus fever**.

blocks.title: Diagnosing SBP
items: Ascitic **neutrophils > 250 × 10⁶/L** (> 250/mm³) almost always means infection
Culture ascites in **blood-culture bottles** before antibiotics
In a bloody tap, subtract 1 neutrophil per 250 red cells
**Several organisms** on culture → suspect a perforated viscus (secondary peritonitis)
Tap any patient with ascites who deteriorates, even without pain or fever

blocks.title: Treating and preventing SBP
items: Start broad-spectrum antibiotics at once, e.g. **cefotaxime** or piperacillin/tazobactam
Give **IV albumin** with the antibiotics; it improves survival
Stop non-selective β-blockers after SBP (they raise the risk of renal failure)
Secondary prophylaxis: **norfloxacin 400 mg/day** if ascites persists
Primary prophylaxis if ascitic protein is low (< 10 g/L) or liver disease is severe; all cirrhotics with a GI bleed get antibiotics
A first SBP episode is an indication for **transplant assessment**

blocks.text: SBP carries a **50% one-year mortality** after the first episode, and about 70% recur within a year.

**Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS)** affects about **10% of advanced cirrhotics with ascites**. Arterial underfilling from vasodilatation causes intense **renal vasoconstriction**. It is **functional** renal failure: the tubules still concentrate urine and kidney histology is almost normal.

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.title: Two types of HRS
rows: Advanced cirrhosis with ascites, often after a precipitant such as SBP

blocks.title: Diagnostic features
items: Cirrhosis with ascites and acute kidney injury
**No proteinuria**; urine sodium **< 10 mmol/24 h**; urine:plasma osmolality > 1.5
No improvement after stopping diuretics and expanding volume with albumin
Exclude shock, nephrotoxins and intrinsic kidney disease first

blocks.title: Precipitants
items: Over-vigorous diuretics
NSAIDs (and aminoglycosides)
Diarrhoea or GI bleeding
Large-volume paracentesis
Infection, especially SBP

blocks.title: Treatment
items: Stop diuretics and correct hypovolaemia, preferably with albumin
**IV albumin + terlipressin** (octreotide + midodrine, or noradrenaline, where terlipressin is not used) – works in about two-thirds
Routine haemodialysis does **not** improve outcome; at most a bridge
Survivors should be assessed for **liver transplantation**; TIPSS can also help

blocks.text: Response to vasoconstrictor + albumin: Davidson says about **two-thirds**, Kumar about **50%**. Use Davidson.
SBP can present as **confusion and fever alone**. A soft abdomen does not exclude it – tap the ascites.

**Hepatic encephalopathy** is a neuropsychiatric syndrome of liver disease that runs from delirium to coma. The main driver is **ammonia from gut bacteria**, which escapes clearance because hepatocytes fail and portosystemic collaterals bypass the liver. Aromatic amino acids rise and branched-chain ones fall.

blocks.title: Clinical grade (Davidson Box 22.9)
rows: Poor concentration, slurred speech, disturbed sleep
Marked delirium; responds to voice or pain

blocks.title: Signs
items: **Asterixis** (flapping tremor) and **constructional apraxia** – cannot copy a five-pointed star
Fetor hepaticus, sleep reversal, slow trail-making test
Later: increased tone, hyper-reflexia, extensor plantars
**Focal neurological signs suggest another cause**

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.title: Precipitants
items: Sedatives, opiates, antidepressants
Dehydration from diuretics or paracentesis; **hypokalaemia**
**Constipation**
Infection, including SBP
Raised protein load, including **GI bleeding**
Portosystemic shunts or TIPSS; development of HCC

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.title: Differential diagnosis
items: Subdural or extradural haematoma (alcoholics who fall)
Drug or alcohol intoxication, delirium tremens
Wernicke's encephalopathy
Hypoglycaemia
Neurological Wilson's disease
Post-ictal state, psychiatric illness

blocks.title: Diagnosis and treatment
items: Diagnosis is **clinical**; EEG shows slowing of alpha waves progressing to delta waves
Treat the precipitant first
**Lactulose 15–30 mL three times daily**, titrated to **two soft motions a day**; it acidifies the colon and reduces ammonia absorption
**Rifaximin 400 mg three times daily** is added or substituted
Routine protein restriction is no longer advised (never beyond 48 h); avoid neomycin

blocks.text: **Arterial ammonia** is usually high but can be raised without encephalopathy, so it adds little to diagnosis or monitoring.

blocks.title: Other complications of cirrhosis
rows: Intrapulmonary vascular dilatation → PaO₂ < 9.3 kPa; desaturation on standing (orthodeoxia), clubbing; contrast echo shows late shunting; treated by transplant (higher risk if PaO₂ < 6.7 kPa)
1–2%; raised pulmonary vascular resistance, normal wedge pressure; severe disease contraindicates transplant
Can trigger decompensation; check with Doppler ultrasound
Usually right-sided; avoid a chest drain

blocks.title: Systemic effects of cirrhosis
rows: Acute decompensation with organ failure; about 31% of cirrhosis admissions; high short-term mortality
Muscle wasting from protein loss; regular meals with a high-protein, low-salt diet; DXA scan for osteoporosis
See HCC section; bacteraemia and SBP are common

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease
Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.text: Cirrhosis causes a **rebalanced** coagulopathy: a high INR does not mean the patient will bleed, so FFP and platelets are not given routinely.

HCC is the **commonest primary liver cancer**; **75–90% arise in cirrhotic livers**. Chronic hepatitis B multiplies the risk about **100-fold**. Annual risk is about **0.4% without cirrhosis and 2–6% with cirrhosis**, and HBeAg-positive carriers have four times the risk of HBeAg-negative ones.

blocks.title: Other risk factors
items: Hepatitis C (HCC arises only once cirrhosis is present)
Alcohol, NASH, haemochromatosis, diabetes
**Aflatoxin** (a fungal metabolite found in groundnuts)
Androgenic steroids

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.title: Presentation
items: A known cirrhotic suddenly **deteriorates**: worse ascites, jaundice or a variceal bleed
Weight loss, anorexia, fever, right upper quadrant pain
Hepatomegaly or a mass, sometimes with an arterial **bruit**
Rupture → intraperitoneal bleeding; a **bloody ascitic tap** in a cirrhotic is HCC in a third

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.title: Diagnosis
items: **AFP** is raised in about 60% (normal < 10 ng/mL) and is often normal with small tumours
A **steadily rising AFP or AFP > 400 ng/mL** warrants an aggressive search for HCC
Contrast CT/MRI: **hypervascular lesion with arterial enhancement and venous-phase washout**
Use **at least two imaging modalities** to confirm and stage
**Avoid biopsy** in possible transplant or resection candidates – < 2% risk of needle-track seeding

blocks.text: **Surveillance**: ultrasound ± AFP **every 6 months** for cirrhosis due to HBV, HCV, alcohol, NASH, haemochromatosis or α1-antitrypsin deficiency – and for **chronic hepatitis B even without cirrhosis**.

blocks.title: Treatment options
rows: Non-cirrhotic liver (treatment of choice); occasionally Child A without portal hypertension
Within **Milan criteria**: one tumour < 5 cm or up to three < 3 cm
About 75% 5-year survival; also cures the cirrhosis
Contraindicated in decompensated cirrhosis; mainly a holding measure

blocks.text: AFP cut-off differs: Davidson uses **> 400 ng/mL** (or a steady rise); K&C Essentials says **> 200 ng/mL** is strongly suggestive. Remember that AFP is **normal in at least a third** of HCCs.

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.text: HCC responds poorly to conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy; kinase inhibitors (sorafenib, lenvatinib, regorafenib) add only months.

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.note: CT with a large hepatocellular carcinoma (arrows).
Staging algorithm for HCC in cirrhosis: ablation/resection/transplant for early, TACE for intermediate, sorafenib for advanced, supportive care for terminal disease.
Multiphase CT/MRI: bright lesion in the arterial phase that washes out in the portal venous and delayed phases.

blocks.title: Routine care of every cirrhotic patient
items: **Treat the cause** – abstinence from alcohol, antiviral therapy, venesection for haemochromatosis – to halt or partly reverse disease
Nutrition: frequent meals, high-protein, low-sodium diet; no alcohol
Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs; aminoglycosides are contraindicated; paracetamol up to 2 g/day is acceptable
Vaccinate against hepatitis A and B (and influenza)
**HCC surveillance**: ultrasound every 6 months
Variceal screening endoscopy at diagnosis and every 2 years
Recalculate MELD regularly and refer for transplant at the right time

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.title: Indications for transplant assessment (Davidson Box 22.58)
rows: First episode of SBP; diuretic-resistant ascites; recurrent variceal bleeding; HCC < 5 cm; persistent encephalopathy
Bilirubin > 100 µmol/L in PBC; **MELD > 12**; Child–Pugh C
Hepatorenal syndrome, hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension

blocks.title: UK listing rules
items: Projected **5-year survival after transplant > 50%**, plus one of:
Category 1: predicted 1-year mortality without transplant > 9% (UKELD > 49)
Category 2: HCC within size limits and without macrovascular invasion
Category 3: variant syndromes such as diuretic-resistant ascites, hepatopulmonary syndrome or intractable pruritus

blocks.title: Contraindications
items: Sepsis outside the hepatobiliary tree
Extrahepatic malignancy; liver metastases other than neuroendocrine
Active alcohol or substance misuse (alcohol-related disease needs proven abstinence, usually 6 months)
Marked cardiorespiratory disease, including severe portopulmonary hypertension
Lack of commitment; older age (usually not offered at ≥ 70, some texts say > 65)

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.title: Matching and waiting
items: Donor and recipient are matched for **ABO group and size**; **HLA matching is not needed**
About 10% of listed patients die while waiting

blocks.title: After transplantation
rows: Tacrolimus or ciclosporin with prednisolone and azathioprine or mycophenolate
60–80%, typically day 5–10; 3 days of IV methylprednisolone
Common in first 3 months; valganciclovir prophylaxis for at-risk recipients
"Vanishing bile duct syndrome", 6 weeks–9 months; often needs re-transplant
HCV, PSC and HCC can recur in the graft

blocks.text: A **first episode of SBP** on its own is enough to trigger transplant assessment.

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

blocks.text: MELD trigger differs: Davidson assesses at **MELD > 12**, Pocket Medicine at ≥ 15, and Kumar refers end-stage disease at MELD ≥ 20 / UKELD ≥ 49 / Child C. Quote Davidson.

cards.front: Histological definition of cirrhosis?
cards.back: Diffuse fibrosis of the liver with regenerative nodule formation.

cards.front: Which cell lays down collagen in hepatic fibrosis?
cards.back: The activated hepatic stellate cell (space of Disse), which becomes myofibroblast-like.

cards.front: Micronodular cirrhosis: nodule size (Davidson) and typical cause?
cards.back: About 1 mm; alcohol.

cards.front: Young patient with cirrhosis: which two extra tests must be checked?
cards.back: Copper/caeruloplasmin (Wilson's) and α1-antitrypsin level.

cards.front: What proportion of healthy people have one or two spider telangiectasias?
cards.back: About 2% (also seen in pregnancy).

cards.front: Child–Pugh class cut-offs?
Requirements for safe percutaneous liver biopsy?
cards.back: PT prolonged < 4 s and platelets > 80 × 10⁹/L; otherwise use the transjugular route.

cards.front: Prolonged PT that does not correct with vitamin K suggests?
cards.back: Severe hepatocellular damage (not vitamin K deficiency).

cards.front: Normal HVPG, and thresholds for significant portal hypertension and bleeding risk?
cards.back: Normal 5–6 mmHg; significant > 10 mmHg; bleeding risk rises > 12 mmHg.

cards.front: Primary prophylaxis of varices: drug and target?
cards.back: Propranolol 80–160 mg/day (or nadolol/carvedilol), aiming for a 25% fall in heart rate; banding if intolerant.

cards.front: Terlipressin regimen in acute variceal bleeding (Davidson)?
cards.back: 2 mg IV four times daily until bleeding stops, then 1 mg four times daily for up to 72 h.

cards.front: Sengstaken–Blakemore tube: gastric balloon volume and oesophageal balloon limit?
cards.back: Gastric 200–250 mL air; oesophageal ≤ 40 mmHg, deflated 10 min every 3 h. Intubate first.

cards.front: What does a SAAG > 11 g/L mean?
cards.back: Portal hypertension is the cause of the ascites (about 96% predictive).

cards.front: Definition of refractory ascites?
cards.back: No response to spironolactone 400 mg + furosemide 160 mg daily, or unable to tolerate them.

cards.front: Albumin replacement with large-volume paracentesis?
cards.back: 6–8 g per litre drained (about 100 mL of 20–25% HAS per 1.5–2 L).

cards.front: Ascitic neutrophil count diagnostic of SBP?
Secondary prophylaxis after SBP with ongoing ascites?
cards.back: Norfloxacin 400 mg/day.

cards.front: Urine findings in hepatorenal syndrome?
cards.back: No proteinuria, urine sodium < 10 mmol/24 h, urine:plasma osmolality > 1.5.

cards.front: First-line treatment of type 1 HRS?
cards.back: IV albumin plus terlipressin (or octreotide + midodrine); transplant assessment for survivors.

cards.front: Lactulose target in hepatic encephalopathy?
cards.back: Titrate (15–30 mL three times daily) to two soft bowel motions a day.

cards.front: Hepatopulmonary syndrome: definition and bedside clue?
cards.back: Hypoxaemia (PaO₂ < 9.3 kPa) from intrapulmonary vascular dilatation; oxygen saturation falls on standing.

cards.front: Milan criteria for transplant in HCC?
cards.back: A single tumour < 5 cm, or up to three tumours each < 3 cm.

cards.front: AFP level that warrants an aggressive search for HCC (Davidson)?
cards.back: > 400 ng/mL, or a steadily rising AFP (normal < 10 ng/mL).

cards.front: MELD score that triggers transplant assessment (Davidson)?
cards.back: MELD > 12.

cards.front: Acute cellular rejection after liver transplant: timing and treatment?
cards.back: Usually day 5–10; 3 days of IV methylprednisolone.

questions.leadIn: Match each case to the best-fitting option. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 19-year-old student has abnormal liver tests and a hard, irregular liver edge. Slit-lamp examination shows golden-brown rings at the corneal margin. Viral serology is negative.
items.explanation: Cirrhosis in a young person with corneal (Kayser–Fleischer) rings is Wilson's disease. Caeruloplasmin and copper should always be checked in young cirrhotics.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman with long-standing itching has a cholestatic liver profile and early cirrhosis on Fibroscan. Antimitochondrial antibody is strongly positive.
items.explanation: AMA positivity is the screening marker for primary biliary cholangitis, a biliary cause of cirrhosis.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man with marked skin pigmentation is found to have cirrhosis. HBsAg and HCV antibody are negative, autoantibodies are negative and he drinks little alcohol. Ferritin and transferrin saturation are both very high.
items.explanation: Two steps: viral and alcohol causes are excluded, and the high ferritin and transferrin saturation with pigmentation point to haemochromatosis. Pigmentation is most striking in this cause.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has: no encephalopathy, bilirubin 45 µmol/L, albumin 31 g/L, PT prolonged by 3 seconds and mild ascites.
questions.leadIn: What is his Child–Pugh class?
questions.explanation: Score each item: encephalopathy none = 1; bilirubin 34–50 = 2; albumin 28–35 = 2; PT < 4 s = 1; mild ascites = 2. Total 8, which falls in the 7–9 band = Child B.
whyNot: Class A needs a total below 7; this patient scores 8.
Seven would require one fewer point – albumin and bilirubin each score 2 here.
Nine would need one more point, e.g. PT 4–6 s prolonged.
Class C needs more than 9 points.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with cirrhosis has several features on examination.
questions.leadIn: Which feature most suggests that alcohol is the cause of his cirrhosis?
questions.explanation: Florid spider naevi, gynaecomastia and parotid swelling are most typical of alcoholic cirrhosis. The other signs occur in cirrhosis of any cause.
whyNot: Palmar erythema reflects a hyperdynamic circulation and occurs in many conditions, even pregnancy.
Splenomegaly reflects portal hypertension of any cause.
Clubbing is a non-specific feature of chronic liver disease.
Ascites signals advanced disease of any cause.

questions.leadIn: Match each case to the best-fitting option. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman with newly diagnosed cirrhosis has large oesophageal varices at screening endoscopy. They have never bled. She has severe asthma.
items.explanation: Primary prevention is a non-selective β-blocker or banding. Asthma rules out β-blockers, so band ligation is chosen.

items.stem: A 63-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with haematemesis from oesophageal varices. Terlipressin is not available in the hospital where he is treated.
items.explanation: A vasoactive drug is needed to lower portal pressure. Where terlipressin is not available, octreotide is the usual alternative.

items.stem: A 58-year-old cirrhotic is admitted with a variceal bleed. Fluids, a vasoactive drug and endoscopy are arranged. A medical student asks which further drug reduces infection and improves survival.
items.explanation: Sepsis is common after a variceal bleed; prophylactic antibiotics (e.g. IV cephalosporin) reduce SBP and improve outcome.

questions.leadIn: Match each case to the best-fitting option. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 75-year-old man with a previous myocardial infarction has ascites, ankle oedema and bibasal crackles. Ascitic SAAG is 16 g/L and total protein 32 g/L.
items.explanation: High SAAG means portal-type hypertension; high protein (> 25 g/L) argues against cirrhosis. With the cardiac history and pulmonary crackles, cardiac failure fits best.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man who drinks heavily has had two attacks of severe epigastric pain this year. Ascitic SAAG is 6 g/L and ascitic amylase is 2800 U/L.
items.explanation: Low SAAG with ascitic amylase above 1000 U/L identifies pancreatic ascites.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman has a slowly enlarging abdomen. The tap yields milky fluid with a triglyceride level of 2.4 g/L.
items.explanation: Triglyceride above 1.1 g/L defines chylous ascites (often lymphatic obstruction).

questions.theme: Acute complications in a patient with cirrhotic ascites
questions.leadIn: Match each case to the best-fitting option. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with cirrhotic ascites becomes confused and febrile. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. Ascitic neutrophil count is 600 × 10⁶/L; Gram stain shows a single type of Gram-negative rod.
items.explanation: Two steps: confusion + fever without abdominal signs is how a third of SBP cases present; neutrophils > 250 × 10⁶/L with a single enteric organism confirms SBP.

items.stem: A 54-year-old woman with cirrhosis and ascites has a rising creatinine over 5 days and is passing very little urine. There is no proteinuria, urine sodium is < 10 mmol/24 h, and renal function does not improve after stopping diuretics and giving albumin.
items.explanation: Rapid, progressive renal failure with intact tubular function and no response to volume = type 1 HRS.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man with cirrhotic ascites has severe abdominal pain. Ascitic culture grows E. coli, Bacteroides and enterococci.
items.explanation: Several organisms, including anaerobes, suggest a perforated viscus – secondary, not spontaneous, peritonitis.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with cirrhosis is brought in by her husband. She is drowsy but opens her eyes and answers when her name is called, and she is lethargic. She has a flapping tremor.
questions.leadIn: What grade of hepatic encephalopathy is this?
questions.explanation: Drowsy but rousable and lethargic is grade 2. Grade 3 implies marked delirium; grade 4 is unconsciousness.
whyNot: She has clear clinical signs, so encephalopathy is present.
Grade 1 is poor concentration, slurred speech and disturbed sleep, without drowsiness.
Grade 3 involves marked delirium with response only to voice or pain.
Grade 4 means no response to voice.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis is found confused at home after a fall. He has asterixis, and a new weakness of the left arm and leg.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: Focal neurological signs point away from simple hepatic encephalopathy. In a drinker who has fallen, a subdural haematoma must be excluded with CT.
whyNot: Ammonia can be raised without encephalopathy and would not explain focal signs.
EEG slowing supports encephalopathy but cannot exclude a haematoma.
Lumbar puncture does not look for the intracranial bleed that new focal signs in a drinker who has fallen suggest.
Caeruloplasmin is for Wilson's disease, not an acute focal deficit.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis (Child–Pugh A) has a new 3.5 cm liver lesion on surveillance ultrasound. He is otherwise fit and could be a transplant candidate.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Davidson advises at least two imaging modalities (CT or MRI after ultrasound). A hypervascular lesion with washout confirms HCC without biopsy.
whyNot: Biopsy should be avoided in transplant or resection candidates because of needle-track seeding.
A new lesion in a cirrhotic needs work-up now, not routine surveillance.
AFP is normal in a third or more of HCCs, so it cannot exclude the diagnosis.
Sorafenib is for advanced disease, and the diagnosis is not yet confirmed.

questions.stem: Four patients with cirrhosis and HCC are discussed at a transplant meeting. None has vascular invasion or spread outside the liver.
questions.leadIn: Which patient falls within the Milan criteria?
questions.explanation: Milan criteria: one tumour < 5 cm, or up to three tumours each < 3 cm. Only the single 4.5 cm lesion qualifies; 5-year survival is about 75%.
whyNot: A single tumour must be < 5 cm.
With more than one tumour, each must be < 3 cm.
Each of three tumours must be < 3 cm.
No more than three tumours are allowed.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman with cirrhosis from hepatitis B is otherwise well. She is admitted with her first episode of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which responds to treatment.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate long-term step?
options: Start primary prophylaxis with propranolol only
questions.explanation: A first SBP episode is a Davidson indication for transplant assessment (Box 22.58); one-year mortality after it is about 50%.
whyNot: β-blockers are for varices and should actually be stopped after SBP.
Variceal screening is every 2 years and does not address her prognosis.
Routine protein restriction is not recommended.
Haemodialysis has no role here.

questions.stem: Seven days after a liver transplant for alcohol-related cirrhosis, a 52-year-old man has a rise in bilirubin and transaminases. Doppler shows a patent hepatic artery.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Acute cellular rejection affects 60–80% of recipients, typically days 5–10, and responds to three days of IV methylprednisolone.
whyNot: Re-transplant is for hepatic artery thrombosis (artery is patent) or chronic ductopenic rejection.
Valganciclovir is CMV prophylaxis, not rejection treatment.
Stopping immunosuppression would worsen rejection.
Nothing suggests a biliary obstruction.

questions.leadIn: Match each case to the best-fitting option. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man taking spironolactone for ascites develops painful breast swelling. His ascites is still present.
items.explanation: Amiloride 5–10 mg/day replaces spironolactone when it causes painful gynaecomastia (or hyperkalaemia).

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has recovered from SBP but her ascites persists. Which drug reduces the chance of another episode?
items.explanation: Norfloxacin 400 mg/day is Davidson's secondary prophylaxis after SBP with continuing ascites.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man has medium-to-large oesophageal varices on screening that have never bled. He has no contraindications to any drug.
items.explanation: Propranolol 80–160 mg/day, titrated to cut heart rate by 25%, is first-line primary prevention.

items.stem: A 64-year-old woman has had a second episode of hepatic encephalopathy despite taking lactulose to two soft motions a day. No new precipitant is found.
items.explanation: Two steps: lactulose is already optimised, so the next drug is rifaximin, which is added to or substituted for lactulose.

questions.stem: Hepatic venous pressure gradients are measured in five patients with chronic liver disease.
questions.leadIn: Which value is the lowest at which variceal bleeding risk is said to rise?
questions.explanation: Normal HVPG is 5–6 mmHg; > 10 mmHg is clinically significant portal hypertension; variceal bleeding risk rises above 12 mmHg.
whyNot: 5–6 mmHg is normal.
8 mmHg is below the 10 mmHg threshold for clinically significant portal hypertension.
> 10 mmHg defines clinically significant portal hypertension, not the bleeding threshold.
20 mmHg is not the threshold quoted for bleeding risk.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman has new ascites. Serum albumin is 30 g/L and ascitic albumin 12 g/L; ascitic total protein is 15 g/L.
questions.leadIn: What does this result most strongly indicate?
questions.explanation: SAAG = 30 − 12 = 18 g/L (> 11 g/L), which is about 96% predictive of portal hypertension; low protein fits cirrhosis.
whyNot: Malignant ascites usually has a low SAAG.
TB peritonitis gives a low SAAG and low glucose.
Chylous ascites is milky with triglyceride > 1.1 g/L, and lymphatic obstruction is a low-SAAG cause.
Pancreatic ascites is low-SAAG with a very high amylase.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis and ascites has had worsening oliguria for 4 days, with creatinine rising from 95 to 310 µmol/L. Urinalysis shows no protein, urine sodium is very low, and there is no response to stopping diuretics and giving albumin.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: This is type 1 HRS. Albumin plus terlipressin works in about two-thirds; survivors should be assessed for transplant.
whyNot: Routine haemodialysis does not improve outcome in HRS.
Diuretics worsen arterial underfilling and are stopped.
Saline adds sodium and worsens ascites; albumin is the preferred volume expander.
Paracentesis without albumin can itself precipitate renal failure.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with cirrhotic ascites has abdominal pain and fever. Ascitic fluid is cloudy.
questions.leadIn: Which finding confirms spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
questions.explanation: An ascitic neutrophil count above 250 × 10⁶/L almost always indicates infection; E. coli is the usual organism.
whyNot: SAAG shows portal hypertension, not infection.
Low protein is typical of any cirrhotic ascites.
High amylase indicates pancreatic ascites.
Multiple organisms suggest secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis vomits a large amount of fresh blood. Pulse is 118/min and BP 92/60 mmHg. IV access is secured and blood is cross-matched.
questions.leadIn: Besides resuscitation, which drug should be started before endoscopy?
questions.explanation: Step 1: a cirrhotic with haematemesis has a variceal bleed until proven otherwise. Step 2: Box 22.32 lists a vasoactive drug (terlipressin) to lower portal pressure, with IV antibiotics, before urgent endoscopy and banding. Step 3: terlipressin reduces bleeding and mortality; give 2 mg IV four times daily. Endoscopy then confirms the source, since about 20% bleed from other lesions.
whyNot: β-blockers are for prevention, not a hypotensive active bleed.
Not part of Davidson's emergency variceal bundle.
The coagulopathy of liver disease is not corrected by vitamin K.
Diuretics would worsen hypovolaemia.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with cirrhosis and ascites becomes drowsy with a temperature of 38.2 °C. Her abdomen is distended but not tender. Diagnostic tap: neutrophils 480 × 10⁶/L.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: Step 1: fever and confusion with soft abdomen – a third of SBP cases lack abdominal signs. Step 2: neutrophils > 250 × 10⁶/L confirm SBP. Step 3: start broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (cefotaxime) at once, with albumin. Step 4: after recovery, if ascites persists, norfloxacin prevents recurrence and transplant assessment is due.
whyNot: Norfloxacin is prophylaxis, not treatment of active SBP.
Draining the fluid does not treat the infection; antibiotics must start at once.
Surgery is for secondary peritonitis (multiple organisms), not SBP.
Lactulose treats the encephalopathy but not the infection driving it.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man with cirrhosis has tense ascites despite a no-added-salt diet, spironolactone 400 mg and furosemide 160 mg daily. Sodium is 131 mmol/L and creatinine is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the first-line treatment now?
questions.explanation: Step 1: maximal diuretics have failed – this is refractory ascites by definition. Step 2: Davidson's first-line treatment is large-volume paracentesis, supported with albumin 6–8 g per litre removed. Step 3: TIPSS is an alternative for frequent taps but may worsen encephalopathy and does not prolong life. Step 4: diuretic-resistant ascites is also a reason for transplant assessment.
whyNot: Escalating loop diuretics beyond this risks electrolyte and renal harm.
Water restriction is only indicated when sodium is < 125 mmol/L.
TIPSS is an alternative, not the first-line option.
400 mg is already the maximum dose used to define diuretic resistance.

questions.leadIn: Match each case to the best-fitting option. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.
options: Doppler ultrasound of the portal vein

items.stem: A 46-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with compensated cirrhosis due to NAFLD. She has never had GI bleeding.
items.explanation: Endoscopy to screen for varices is done at diagnosis and repeated every 2 years.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man with previously stable cirrhosis suddenly decompensates with new ascites. The ascitic neutrophil count is 40 × 10⁶/L and a surveillance scan last month showed no liver mass. Which investigation checks for the vascular event that is a recognised trigger of this?
items.explanation: Two steps: the low neutrophil count argues against SBP, and portal vein thrombosis is a recognised cause of decompensation in stable cirrhosis – check portal vein patency with Doppler ultrasound.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man needs histology to stage his liver disease. His PT is prolonged by 7 seconds and his platelet count is 55 × 10⁹/L.
items.explanation: Two steps: histology is needed, but percutaneous biopsy requires PT < 4 s prolonged and platelets > 80 × 10⁹/L – so use the transjugular route.

items.stem: A 50-year-old man with hepatitis C cirrhosis attends routine surveillance. Alongside ultrasound, which blood test is checked every 6 months?
items.explanation: HCC surveillance is ultrasound plus AFP every 6 months.

questions.leadIn: Match each case to the best-fitting option. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman with cirrhosis has clubbing and breathlessness. Her oxygen saturation is 95% lying down but 88% standing. Contrast echocardiography shows bubbles in the left atrium several beats after the right.
items.explanation: Desaturation on standing (orthodeoxia) and late shunting on contrast echo indicate intrapulmonary vascular dilatation – hepatopulmonary syndrome.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis has iron-deficiency anaemia without overt bleeding. Endoscopy shows multiple areas of punctate erythema ("snakeskin" pattern) in the gastric mucosa and no varices.
items.explanation: Snakeskin mucosa causing chronic iron loss is portal hypertensive gastropathy; propranolol is first-line.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman with cirrhosis has a platelet count of 90 × 10⁹/L, a mildly low white count and a palpable spleen. Haemoglobin is normal.
items.explanation: Platelets around 100 × 10⁹/L with splenomegaly reflect hypersplenism from portal hypertension.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis has right-sided breathlessness. Chest X-ray shows a large right effusion; tap shows a transudate with a low protein. He also has ascites.
items.explanation: A right-sided transudate in a patient with ascites is a hepatic hydrothorax (about 10% of patients).

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman with cirrhotic ascites starts spironolactone and a salt-restricted diet. Over 3 days her weight falls by 2.5 kg a day and her creatinine begins to rise.
questions.leadIn: What is the maximum daily weight loss Davidson recommends?
questions.explanation: Weight should not fall by more than 1 kg/day, to avoid renal failure and electrolyte disturbance. Her diuretics should be reduced.
whyNot: Slower than needed; not the quoted ceiling.
Some quick sources aim for about 0.5 kg/day, but Davidson's ceiling is 1 kg/day.
Twice the recommended maximum.
Far above the safe maximum.

cites.chapter: Liver, biliary tract and pancreatic disease

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has chronic hepatitis B. Fibroscan and ultrasound show no cirrhosis; liver tests are normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate HCC surveillance?
questions.explanation: Chronic hepatitis B raises HCC risk even without cirrhosis, so Davidson includes it in 6-monthly ultrasound + AFP surveillance.
whyNot: HBV is the exception – risk is raised even without cirrhosis.
CT is used to characterise lesions, not for routine screening.
AFP alone misses many small tumours.
Biopsy has no role in surveillance.

questions.theme: Treatment of complications of portal hypertension
questions.leadIn: Match each case to the best-fitting option. Any option can be the answer for one case, several cases or none.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man with cirrhosis is bleeding from varices in the gastric fundus seen at urgent endoscopy.
items.explanation: Fundal gastric varices are better treated with cyanoacrylate glue (or thrombin) than banding; glue embolism to the lungs is a risk.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman with cirrhosis has tense, uncomfortable ascites despite spironolactone 400 mg and furosemide 160 mg daily.
items.explanation: This is refractory ascites; first-line is large-volume paracentesis with albumin 6–8 g per litre removed.

items.stem: A 51-year-old man with cirrhosis and SBP develops oliguria over 3 days; creatinine has trebled despite stopping diuretics and giving albumin. Urine has no protein and very little sodium.
items.explanation: Two steps: SBP has precipitated renal failure with HRS features, so treat with albumin plus terlipressin.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with cirrhosis has a PT prolonged by 6 seconds. He is given IV vitamin K, but the PT is unchanged after 24 hours.
questions.leadIn: What is the best explanation?
questions.explanation: In chronic liver disease a long PT reflects poor synthetic function and is not corrected by vitamin K. Vitamin K corrects deficiency, e.g. from biliary obstruction.
whyNot: Cholestatic vitamin K malabsorption would correct with IV vitamin K.
Dietary deficiency would correct with vitamin K.
Warfarin effect is reversed by vitamin K.
A true, uncorrectable PT is expected in severe liver disease.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with cirrhosis has worsening breathlessness and clubbing. Chest X-ray is clear. Arterial PaO₂ is 8.6 kPa, and her oxygen saturation falls when she stands.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hypoxaemia (PaO₂ < 9.3 kPa) from intrapulmonary vascular dilatation with desaturation on standing is hepatopulmonary syndrome. Liver transplant is the definitive treatment.
whyNot: Portopulmonary hypertension is raised pulmonary vascular resistance; orthodeoxia is not its hallmark.
A hydrothorax would show on the chest X-ray.
No acute onset or risk factor is given, and orthodeoxia with clubbing points elsewhere.
Splinting would worsen when lying, not standing.

questions.stem: Five patients with decompensated cirrhosis are referred for liver transplant assessment.
questions.leadIn: Which factor is a contraindication to transplantation?
questions.explanation: Active alcohol or substance misuse is a main contraindication; patients must show they can abstain. The other options are indications for assessment.
whyNot: This is an indication for assessment.
This is an indication for assessment.
A small HCC within Milan criteria is an indication.
HPS is an indication (a variant syndrome) and can be treated by transplant.

ospe.identify: Histology series: normal lobule vs bridging fibrosis vs established cirrhosis with regenerative nodules surrounded by fibrous septa.
Cirrhotic liver on collagen stain (nodules within fibrous bands) and on CT (irregular outline, varices, ascites).
CT signs of cirrhosis with portal hypertension: shrunken irregular liver, splenomegaly, ascites and gastric collaterals.
Endoscopy: oesophageal varices, gastric varices, and the appearance after band ligation.
Sengstaken–Blakemore tube: gastric balloon (inflate first, 200–250 mL air), oesophageal balloon (≤ 40 mmHg) and aspiration ports.
Radiograph of a TIPSS stent linking the portal vein to the hepatic vein; complications include encephalopathy.
CT: large hepatocellular carcinoma within the liver.
Multiphase imaging of HCC: arterial-phase enhancement followed by washout in the portal venous and delayed phases.
